categories.justification: The output answers the actual decision and covers all four mustFlag issues: the gateway's R1 gap, the vendor benchmark run without mTLS, sidecar mode breaking the budget, and node-proxy as a viable option. It also covers R2 partial coverage, team capacity and audit evidence, without padding.
quotes: Neither option, as you framed it, meets your approved requirements.
Recommendation: choose Lattice this quarter, but deploy it in node-proxy mode, not sidecar mode.

categories.justification: I checked every source-derived fact and figure against the four supplied documents and all are correct: 2.6/0.9 ms, 13/4.5 ms, 0.8 ms, the 2027-06-30 deadline, GA since 3.2, per-route ingress limits, and the derived 6.5x, 23% and 47%. One product-specific claim, that services can be onboarded without restarts, has no support in the sources and only falls under a blanket 'general engineering knowledge' disclaimer.
quotes: Your own load test measured 2.6 ms p99 per hop, which comes to about 13 ms over 5 hops against a 10 ms budget.
services can be onboarded without restarting them for injection

categories.justification: Explains why the vendor and internal numbers differ (mTLS, payload size, telemetry, load). Quantifies every configuration, discusses whether p99s add up across hops, and covers specific failure modes: node-proxy blast radius, same-node encryption, connection churn, retries, growth.
quotes: Adding p99s together is a deliberately conservative heuristic.
A crash or overload of one node proxy affects every pod on that node.

categories.justification: Rejects the user's 'latency shouldn't be a concern' premise and questions the two-option framing. It answers counterarguments fairly, including that summing p99s may overstate latency, and says what would change the conclusion: an end-to-end test, or library-level mTLS if the mesh is blocked.
quotes: The claim that "latency shouldn't be a concern" rests on a vendor benchmark run with **mTLS disabled**.
"Node-proxy wasn't one of the two options." It is the same product, it is GA, and it is in your own test.

categories.justification: Gives a clear bottom line, conditional fallbacks and concrete next steps: an end-to-end checkout test, a vendor check on per-tenant limits, collecting audit evidence, and recording the decision in the architecture log.
quotes: Run an end-to-end checkout load test (edge plus 5 hops, real payloads, at or above peak rps) to replace the sum-of-p99s estimate.
Check with Lattice whether its ingress can rate-limit per tenant

categories.justification: Well organised, with a requirement table, a quantitative table and the arithmetic shown. Sources are listed with what each supports, and remaining uncertainty and limitations have their own labelled section.
quotes: The internal results come from a single test with no variance or confidence interval reported

notesForHumanAdjudicator: I checked the output against the four supplied source files in the run directory. All facts drawn from them are accurate, and both numeric checks match the reference: V1 = 13.0 ms and V2 = 4.5 ms. No mustNotClaim pattern appears; the 0.4 ms figure is explicitly rejected and Portcullis is never said to meet all requirements. I set accuracy one notch down, to 0.75, because the output claims Lattice node-proxy lets services be onboarded without restarts, which the sources do not support and which is covered only by a blanket general-knowledge disclaimer. 1.0 would also be defensible. The recommendation matches the reference: node-proxy mode, with Portcullis or Lattice ingress at the edge, and library-level mTLS as the fallback.
